source.title: A Priori Estimates of the Generalization Error for Two-layer Neural Networks
source.authors: W. E; Chao Ma; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own two-layer-network results on natural-label train and test accuracy under explicit path-norm regularization, a related generalization question. It does not test the specific claim versions about random-label memorization, dropout, optimizer comparisons, batch size, or sharpness.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical population-risk bounds and experiments on regularized versus unregularized networks, widths, and initialization. The width sweep reports path norms rather than test error; initialization results are figure-only. No random-label experiment is reported.
record.test_reason: The study tests explicit path-norm regularization and derives population-risk bounds, but none of V1–V8. It reports no random-label experiment, test-error comparison across widths, convolutional comparison, optimizer comparison, batch-size comparison, dropout intervention, magnitude-aware sharpness measurement, or memorized-example removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish nearly optimal a priori population-risk bounds for explicitly regularized two-layer networks, interpret neural networks as adaptive kernel methods, and report broadly comparable regularized and unregularized test accuracies with greater initialization robustness under regularization. They explicitly leave implicit regularization unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use explicit path-norm regularization and Adam; the paper does not use the random-label memorization recipe or interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that performance varies with initialization variance in Figure 6.2; it says regularized models are more stable and perform significantly better for large initialization. In Table 6.1, the effect of explicit regularization differs between CIFAR-10 and MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: At width 10,000, path-norm regularization changes CIFAR-10 test accuracy from 84.5% to 86.9% and MNIST accuracy from 98.8% to 97.8%, while lowering training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit path-norm regularization leaves test accuracy broadly comparable on these binary image tasks, with different directions of change across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 6.1 shows normalized path norm increasing with width without regularization and remaining nearly constant with regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit path-norm regularization controls the width dependence of the norm-based generalization bound in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.2 reports more stable test accuracy across initialization variances with regularization and better performance at large initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit path-norm regularization reduces sensitivity to initialization in the tested width-10,000, sample-size-100 networks.

record.problems: The experiments are limited to two binary classification datasets and one reported network width in Table 6.1; table results give means over 5 repetitions without an error measure. Width comparisons for path norm and initialization comparisons for test accuracy are shown in figures, not as recoverable table values. The study does not test random-label memorization.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numerical experiment rows extracted. Figure 6.1 reports path norm across widths, not test error; Figure 6.2 reports test accuracy by initialization variance but values are figure-only.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and coexistence with natural-label generalization under the same recipe.

Test error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation. Figure 6.1 measures path norm; decreasing theoretical risk bounds for explicitly regularized estimators do not establish the claimed empirical trend.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning. Adam is used without an optimizer comparator.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against alternative measures. Path norms and their bounds are different measures.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, not because their accuracy values are unreadable. Table 6.1 also contains sample-size-100 accuracy results and normalized path norms omitted from the record; these do not bear on a listed version and therefore are not version-specific missing results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy; the same recipe's performance on natural versus random labels.
Test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold; the width sweep reports path norm.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch comparisons and recipe adaptations.
Dropout comparisons and the effect of removing dropout and weight decay together.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
